title: Recurring NEET concepts: 2016–2025
scope: Selected recurring concepts across one available English or bilingual booklet per year, 2016–2025. 2016 uses Phase II; additional sittings and retests are excluded. Evidence lists examples, not complete counts or a prediction of future questions. No exhaustive exact-text duplicate audit is claimed.

questions.prompt: A metal has a work function of 3.6 eV. Light supplies photons of energy 8.1 eV. What stopping-potential magnitude is needed to stop the fastest emitted electrons?
questions.explanation: Einstein's equation gives Kmax = 8.1 − 3.6 = 4.5 eV. Since eVs = Kmax, the stopping-potential magnitude is 4.5 V.

questions.prompt: Monochromatic light has frequency 0.90 times a metal's threshold frequency. Its intensity is then tripled without changing frequency. In the ordinary single-photon photoelectric model, what happens?
choices: Emission starts because intensity is higher
questions.explanation: Each photon's energy remains below the work function. Increasing intensity increases the number of photons, not the energy of each photon.

questions.prompt: An isotope's half-life is 18 minutes. What percentage of its initial undecayed nuclei remains after 72 minutes?
questions.explanation: 72/18 = 4 half-lives. The remaining fraction is (1/2)^4 = 1/16, or 6.25%.

questions.prompt: A radioactive sample's activity falls from 960 counts per minute to 120 counts per minute in 60 minutes. What is its half-life?
questions.explanation: The activity falls to 1/8 = (1/2)^3. Three half-lives take 60 minutes, so one half-life is 20 minutes.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.title: Hydrogen energy levels and spectral series

questions.prompt: Use En = −13.6/n² eV for hydrogen. What photon energy is emitted when an electron moves from n = 4 to n = 2?
questions.explanation: E4 = −0.85 eV and E2 = −3.40 eV. The emitted photon carries E4 − E2 = 2.55 eV; this transition belongs to the Balmer series.

questions.prompt: A hydrogen atom is initially in its n = 2 state. Using En = −13.6/n² eV, what minimum energy ionises it from that state?
questions.explanation: The n = 2 energy is −3.4 eV. Reaching the ionisation limit at 0 eV requires 3.4 eV.

questions.prompt: An 8 μF capacitor at 24 V is disconnected from its battery and connected in parallel to an uncharged 4 μF capacitor. With like terminals joined, what is the final common voltage?
questions.explanation: Charge is conserved: Qinitial = 8 × 24 = 192 μC. Total capacitance is 12 μF, so Vfinal = 192/12 = 16 V.

questions.prompt: A 10 μF capacitor charged to 40 V is isolated and connected in parallel to an identical uncharged capacitor. What electrostatic energy remains after redistribution?
questions.explanation: The final voltage is 20 V and combined capacitance is 20 μF. Ufinal = ½ × 20 × 10⁻⁶ × 20² = 0.004 J = 4 mJ.

questions.prompt: A 0.36 kg mass oscillates on an ideal spring with stiffness 100 N m⁻¹. What is its period?
A spring of stiffness 150 N m⁻¹ is extended by 4.0 cm within its elastic range. How much elastic potential energy is stored?
questions.explanation: Convert extension to 0.040 m. U = ½kx² = ½ × 150 × 0.040² = 0.120 J.

questions.prompt: Thin lenses of powers +8 D and −3 D are placed in contact in air. What is the equivalent focal length?
questions.explanation: For thin lenses in contact, Ptotal = +8 − 3 = +5 D. Hence f = 1/P = +0.20 m.

questions.prompt: A convex lens of focal length +15 cm is placed in contact with a concave lens of focal length −30 cm. What is the combination's focal length?
questions.explanation: 1/F = 1/15 − 1/30 = 1/30 cm⁻¹. Thus F = +30 cm, so the combination is converging.

questions.prompt: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 12 seconds. How long does it take for 87.5% of the reactant to disappear?
questions.explanation: 87.5% disappearance leaves 12.5% = 1/8. That is three half-lives: 3 × 12 = 36 s.

questions.prompt: A first-order reaction has rate constant 0.020 s⁻¹. How long is needed for the reactant concentration to fall to 10% of its initial value? Use ln 10 = 2.303.
questions.explanation: The integrated law is t = ln([A]0/[A]t)/k. Therefore t = ln 10/0.020 = 115.15 s.

questions.prompt: For a reaction, ΔH = +24.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +80.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Treat both as constant. At which temperatures is ΔG negative?
questions.explanation: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Convert ΔH to 24000 J mol⁻¹; ΔG < 0 when T > 24000/80 = 300 K. At 300 K, ΔG is zero.

questions.prompt: A standard cell transfers two moles of electrons per mole of reaction and has E°cell = +0.350 V. With F = 96500 C mol⁻¹, what is ΔG°?
An ideal dilute solution contains a non-electrolyte at molality 0.150 mol kg⁻¹. The solvent has Kf = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹. What is the freezing-point depression?
questions.explanation: For a non-electrolyte, i = 1. ΔTf = iKfm = 1 × 1.86 × 0.150 = 0.279 K.

questions.prompt: At 300 K, an ideal dilute non-electrolyte solution has concentration 0.0300 mol L⁻¹. Using R = 0.0820 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, find its osmotic pressure.
questions.explanation: π = cRT = 0.0300 × 0.0820 × 300 = 0.738 atm; i = 1 for the stated non-electrolyte.

questions.prompt: A central atom has three bonding pairs and one lone pair in a four-domain VSEPR arrangement. What molecular shape is predicted?
questions.explanation: Four electron domains have tetrahedral electron-pair geometry. With one lone pair, the positions of the three bonded atoms give a trigonal pyramidal molecular shape.

questions.prompt: XeF4 has four Xe–F bonds and two lone pairs on xenon. Which molecular shape follows from its six electron domains?
questions.explanation: Six domains adopt an octahedral electron-domain arrangement. The two lone pairs occupy opposite positions, leaving four F atoms in a square plane.

questions.prompt: Each ethane-1,2-diamine ligand (en) bonds through two nitrogen atoms. What is chromium's coordination number in [Cr(en)3]³⁺?
questions.explanation: Three bidentate en ligands provide 3 × 2 = 6 donor atoms bonded to chromium. Coordination number counts donor atoms, not the number of ligand molecules.

questions.prompt: Which complex contains only one type of coordinated ligand and is therefore homoleptic?
questions.explanation: [Co(NH3)6]³⁺ has only ammine ligands. Each other listed complex contains two ligand types and is heteroleptic.

questions.prompt: Two labelled pure samples contain propanal and propanone. Under the usual Tollens' test conditions, which sample can reduce the reagent to give a silver mirror?
questions.explanation: Propanal is an aldehyde and is oxidised while Ag(I) is reduced to silver. The ordinary ketone propanone does not give the usual positive Tollens' test.

questions.prompt: A lab technician prepares the blue Fehling's A stock solution before mixing it with Fehling's B. Which solute supplies the copper(II) ions in solution A?
questions.explanation: Fehling's A is aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Fehling's B supplies alkaline sodium potassium tartrate; the two solutions are mixed for the test.

questions.prompt: Consider 5′-GAATTC-3′ paired with 3′-CTTAAG-5′. What makes this double-stranded DNA site palindromic?
choices: Both strands have the same sequence when read 5′ to 3′
Both strands have the same sequence when read left to right
questions.explanation: Read the lower strand from right to left to follow its 5′ → 3′ direction: GAATTC. Matching sequences in the same directional reading define this DNA palindrome.

questions.prompt: A cloning experiment has already produced compatible sticky ends in a vector and insert. Which enzyme seals the sugar-phosphate backbone after their ends pair?
questions.explanation: DNA ligase forms phosphodiester bonds to seal nicks in the backbone. Restriction enzymes perform cutting; ligase performs joining.

questions.prompt: An ideal PCR starts with three double-stranded target DNA molecules. With perfect doubling in each cycle, how many target molecules are present after five cycles?
questions.explanation: With ideal amplification, Nfinal = Ninitial × 2^n. Thus 3 × 2^5 = 96 double-stranded target molecules.

questions.prompt: During the first high-temperature step of PCR, what change allows primers to bind in the following step?
choices: DNA strands separate as base-pair hydrogen bonds are disrupted
All phosphodiester bonds in the target are destroyed
Primers are converted into amino acids
DNA ligase joins the two template strands
questions.explanation: Denaturation separates complementary strands without destroying the template backbone. Primers then anneal on cooling, followed by polymerase extension.

questions.prompt: In an otherwise functional lac operon, a mutation prevents the repressor from binding the operator. If glucose repression is absent, what is expected even when lactose is absent?
choices: The structural genes can be transcribed
questions.explanation: The repressor normally blocks transcription in the absence of inducer. Failure to bind the operator removes that block, permitting constitutive expression under the stated conditions.

questions.prompt: A mutation disrupts lacY while lacZ remains functional. Which function is directly affected?
choices: Membrane transport of lactose by permease
questions.explanation: lacY codes for permease, which facilitates lactose entry. lacZ codes for β-galactosidase, while lacA codes for transacetylase.

questions.prompt: Bacteria with fully ¹⁵N-labelled DNA are transferred to ¹⁴N medium. After two generations of semiconservative replication, what proportions of DNA molecules are hybrid and light?
questions.explanation: Generation one produces all hybrid DNA. In generation two, each hybrid molecule makes one hybrid and one light molecule, giving equal proportions.

questions.prompt: Why does the lagging strand form short DNA fragments at a replication fork?
choices: DNA polymerase synthesises new DNA only 5′ → 3′ on antiparallel templates
DNA polymerase synthesises the lagging strand only 3′ → 5′
The lagging strand has no template
RNA primers permanently replace all DNA
questions.explanation: Polymerase extends a strand at its 3′ end, so synthesis proceeds 5′ → 3′. On the oppositely oriented template, synthesis occurs discontinuously as Okazaki fragments.

questions.prompt: In a Hardy–Weinberg population with two alleles, the recessive homozygote frequency is 0.09. What is the heterozygote frequency?
questions.explanation: q² = 0.09 gives q = 0.30. Therefore p = 0.70 and heterozygote frequency 2pq = 2 × 0.70 × 0.30 = 0.42.

questions.prompt: A previously isolated population receives many migrants whose allele frequencies differ from its own. Which Hardy–Weinberg assumption has been violated directly?
choices: Two alleles must have identical frequencies
questions.explanation: The no-migration/no-gene-flow assumption is violated. Migration can change the recipient population's allele frequencies.

questions.prompt: A marine ecosystem has a small standing crop of rapidly reproducing phytoplankton and a larger standing biomass of zooplankton. Which statement can be correct?
choices: Both energy and biomass pyramids must be inverted
The biomass pyramid can be inverted while the energy pyramid stays upright
The energy pyramid is inverted whenever producers are small
questions.explanation: Rapid producer turnover can support a greater consumer standing biomass. Energy transfer still loses usable energy at each trophic step, so the energy pyramid remains upright.

questions.prompt: Why is an ecological pyramid of energy upright when energy flow is measured over the same area and time?
choices: Usable energy is lost between successive trophic levels
Consumers receive more energy than producers capture
questions.explanation: Energy is spent in metabolism and dissipated as heat, with other losses during transfer. Less energy is available to each successive trophic level.
